{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-constant-prediction-decompose}
#### Expected squared error of a constant prediction

Let $Y$ be a random variable with mean $\mean$ and finite variance.
Then for every number $c$,

$$
\E{\sqf{Y - c}} = \Var{Y} + \sqf{\mean - c}.
$$ {#eq-constant-prediction-decompose}

:::

::: proof

Add and subtract $\mean$ inside the square,
expand it,
and take the expectation term by term:

$$
\ba
\E{\sqf{Y - c}}
&= \E{\sqf{(Y - \mean) + (\mean - c)}}
&& \text{(add and subtract } \mean \text{)} \\
&= \E{\sqf{Y - \mean} + 2(\mean - c)(Y - \mean) + \sqf{\mean - c}}
&& \text{(expand the square of a sum)} \\
&= \E{\sqf{Y - \mean}} + 2(\mean - c)\E{Y - \mean} + \sqf{\mean - c}
&& \text{(linearity of expectation; } \mean \text{ and } c \text{ are constants)} \\
&= \Var{Y} + 2(\mean - c)\E{Y - \mean} + \sqf{\mean - c}
&& \text{(variance as expected squared deviation)} \\
&= \Var{Y} + 2(\mean - c) \cdot 0 + \sqf{\mean - c}
&& \text{(} \E{Y - \mean} = \E{Y} - \mean = 0 \text{)} \\
&= \Var{Y} + \sqf{\mean - c}
&& \text{(zero times a number)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#cor-best-constant}
#### The mean is the best constant prediction under squared error

Under the assumptions of @thm-constant-prediction-decompose,

$$
\argmin_{c \in \reals} \E{\sqf{Y - c}} = \set{\mean}
\quad \text{and} \quad
\min_{c \in \reals} \E{\sqf{Y - c}} = \Var{Y},
$$

where $\argmin$ is the [set of minimizers](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-basics.html#def-argmin).

:::

::: proof

In @eq-constant-prediction-decompose the first term, $\Var{Y}$, does not depend on $c$.
The second term, $\sqf{\mean - c}$, is a square, so it is never negative,
and it is zero exactly when $c = \mean$.
So $c = \mean$ minimizes the expected squared error and no other number does,
and at $c = \mean$ the expected squared error is $\Var{Y}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-best-constant-auto}
#### The best constant prediction of fuel economy

Take the 392 cars in the Auto data [described on the limit theorems page](limit-theorems.qmd#exm-clt-auto) as the whole population,
and predict the fuel economy (`mpg`) of a car drawn at random with one number $c$.
The code below computes the expected squared error of three constants,
and sets each beside the right side of @eq-constant-prediction-decompose.

```{r}
#| label: best-constant-auto
#| code-fold: false
mpg <- read.csv("data/auto.csv")$mpg
mu <- mean(mpg)
sigma2 <- mean((mpg - mu)^2)

c_values <- c(mean = mu, median = median(mpg), twenty = 20)
data.frame(
  c = c_values,
  expected_squared_error = sapply(c_values, function(cc) mean((mpg - cc)^2)),
  decomposition = sigma2 + (mu - c_values)^2
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# The claims the prose makes: there are 392 cars, the two columns agree, and the mean is best.
squared_error <- sapply(c_values, function(cc) mean((mpg - cc)^2))
stopifnot(
  length(mpg) == 392L,
  !anyNA(mpg),
  all.equal(unname(squared_error), unname(sigma2 + (mu - c_values)^2)),
  which.min(squared_error) == 1,
  all.equal(unname(squared_error[1]), sigma2)
)
```

The two columns agree, as @thm-constant-prediction-decompose says.
The mean, `{r} round(mu, 2)`, has the smallest expected squared error, `{r} round(sigma2, 2)`,
which is the variance of `mpg` over these cars (divisor the number of cars, not one fewer), as @cor-best-constant says;
the median and $c = 20$ are each worse by $\sqf{\mean - c}$.

:::
